tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 36-66. doi:10.5070/H922153559
tone_statements.quote: The tone inventories of Maraic languages are often described as involving three pitch (and in some cases tone) levels. In addition to Senthang, Zophei and Mara are also reported to use three pitch levels, along with contours. Mara makes a lexical contrast between L, M, and H morphemes, with a HM Fall occurring in derived environments (Arden 2010: 49-50, 65).
tone_statements.locator: p. 40, footnote 12 to sect. 3.1 'Pitch pattern inventories' (Table 1 on p. 39)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 level (L, M, H) + HM fall in derived environments

tone_statements.citation: Arden, Michelle J. 2010. A phonetic, phonological, and morphosyntactic analysis of the Mara language. MA thesis, San Jose State University (Master's Theses 3744). doi:10.31979/etd.v36r-dk3u. 179 pp.
tone_statements.quote: The Mara language is primarily a three-tone system, although some exceptions exist. Our speaker characterized the tones as a low- mid-high “do-re-mi” scale. … There is ample evidence that all three tones are contrastive. Despite the prevalence of this three-tone system, some exceptions were found with high-mid contour tones together with what seems to be an unusually long vowel. … The falling tone in Mara is regular but rare in lexical contexts. More commonly, it appears in morphologically derived contexts.
tone_statements.locator: sect. 5.3 'Three-tone System' p. 49; sect. 6.3 'Tones' p. 63; sect. 6.3.1 p. 65

sources.citation: Savidge, Fred W. 1908. A grammar and dictionary of the Lakher language. Allahabad: Pioneer Press. 225 pp.
sources.note: Only 'Lakher alphabet and pronunciation' (pp. 1-2, page scan viewed). Footnote to the asterisked long vowels â ê î ô û: '* The final vowels of words and syllables being generally long, they are not as a rule accented.' — 'accented' here means marked with the circumflex length sign (orthography), not word stress. No word-stress description; no tones recognised.

sources.citation: Löffler, Lorenz G. 2002. Some notes on Maraa. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(1): 123-136. doi:10.15144/LTBA-25.1.123
sources.note: §2 'Phonemes and tones' (pp. 124-127): Maraa has three tones (low, high, mid), 'both Savidge and Lorrain failed to recognize the importance of tones'; 'Lorrain mentions them in his Grammar and Dictionary, but the tones he gives in the few lines devoted to this (p. 59) are mostly wrong' (p. 125). The only 'stress' mentions concern the diphthong /ie/: 'the only diphthong in Maraa with the stress on the second vowel; a Frenchman would have written it /ié/' (p. 126) and 'MM /ie/ (with the stress on a very narrow [e])' (p. 133) — vowel-internal prominence, not word stress. No word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Lorrain, Reginald Arthur. 1951. Grammar and dictionary of the Lakher or Mara language. Gauhati: Government of Assam, Dept. of Historical and Antiquarian Studies. x+372 pp. — ONLY 3 pages (title, introduction, Part I Orthography) as scanned by the Rosetta Project
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, HathiTrust search-only; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 1286.180)
sources.note: Part I Orthography: alphabet, 'All syllables in the Mara language end in a vowel never in a consonant'; 'All the ordinary vowels in Mara.. being long there are only a very few instances where the vowel needs a circumflex accent placed over it to increase the length of that sound' — circumflex 'accent' = vowel length, with a minimal pair of meaning change; nothing on word stress. The full grammar (pp. 1-59; Löffler reports a few lines on tones at p. 59) is not open: HathiTrust catalog lists it 'Limited (search only)'; not on archive.org, Google Books, or DLI.

sources.citation: VanBik, Kenneth. 2009. Proto-Kuki-Chin: A reconstructed ancestor of the Kuki-Chin languages. STEDT Monograph 8. Berkeley: UC Berkeley. 626 pp.
sources.note: Comparative-historical; Mara (Maraic group, §2.3.3, pp. 22-23) treated via sound correspondences (initials, rhymes, tones). a full-text search for stress/accent finds only lexical glosses (e.g. [1292] INTONATION/ACCENT PCC *thluuk, Mara thlu-zi 'a tune'). No statement on Mara word stress.
